case_analysis.focal_point: Whether 26 U.S.C. § 7609(c)(2)(D)(i)’s exception to the IRS’s third‑party summons notice requirement applies whenever a summons may help the IRS collect an assessed tax from a delinquent taxpayer, even if the summons seeks records of innocent third parties with no legal responsibility for that tax.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 26 U.S.C. § 7609 (especially § 7609(a)-(b) (notice and right to petition to quash) and § 7609(c)(2)(D)(i)-(ii) (the 'in aid of collection' exceptions)); raised in amici: Fourth Amendment privacy concerns and the constitutional-avoidance canon.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that the Sixth Circuit’s broad reading of § 7609(c)(2)(D)(i) wrongly eliminates notice and the right to challenge IRS summonses whenever the IRS is collecting an assessment, even when the summons targets bank/financial records of third parties who do not owe the tax and are not legally liable for it. They contend the statutory text, structure, and purpose show the 'in aid of collection' exception should be narrow—limited to situations where the summons is directed at the delinquent taxpayer’s own accounts or at persons/entities holding the taxpayer’s assets (or otherwise liable), so that notice would risk asset dissipation. They emphasize the Sixth (and Seventh) Circuit approach makes key statutory language superfluous (including the reference to the delinquent taxpayer and the separate subparagraph (ii)), collapses the general rule of notice into the exception once an assessment exists, and undermines Congress’s goal of adding procedural protections against undue IRS intrusion. Amici further argue that denying notice for innocent third parties raises serious Fourth Amendment and privacy concerns, supporting a narrower construction under constitutional avoidance.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The IRS argues that § 7609(c)(2)(D)(i) categorically removes the notice and petition-to-quash regime for third-party summonses issued 'in aid of the collection' of an assessed liability, and that this encompasses summonses seeking information about assets or accounts that may be reachable to satisfy the taxpayer’s debt—even if the records belong to third parties (e.g., relatives, associates, or entities) and even if those parties are not themselves the assessed taxpayers. On this view, the summons is 'in aid of collection' so long as it is reasonably issued to locate assets or financial information useful to collecting the delinquency, and requiring notice would impede effective collection by alerting those connected to the taxpayer and enabling concealment or dissipation of assets. The government also contends the lower court’s interpretation is consistent with the statutory scheme and that judicial review can occur through other channels (e.g., enforcement proceedings), making the notice regime unnecessary in this collection context.
key_precedents: United States v. Miller, 425 U.S. 435 (1976) (third-party bank records and Fourth Amendment expectations of privacy; raised by privacy-focused amici)
Carpenter v. United States, 585 U.S. 296 (2018) (limits on the third-party doctrine; invoked by amici to frame modern privacy concerns)
United States v. Powell, 379 U.S. 48 (1964) (standards for enforcing IRS summonses; background to summons enforcement litigation)
Donaldson v. United States, 400 U.S. 517 (1971) (IRS summons authority; background context)
United States v. Arthur Young & Co., 465 U.S. 805 (1984) (breadth of IRS summons power; contextual authority)
Church of Scientology of California v. United States, 506 U.S. 9 (1992) (summons-related procedural issues; often cited in summons litigation context)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito’s practicality point—that notice can tip off targets and that Powell review remains—carries weight, but it cannot overcome the whole-text problem: on the Government’s reading, once there is an assessment, § 7609(c)(2)(D)(i) becomes a near-categorical escape hatch and the limiting phrase “against the person with respect to whose liability the summons is issued” does little work. As Justice Barrett and Justice Thomas emphasize, that construction also threatens to render clause (ii)’s distinct reference to “transferee or fiduciary” largely redundant, which is a serious surplusage and structural concern in a carefully cabined notice-and-quash scheme. Justice Kavanaugh’s reliance on Powell as an adequate back-end safeguard does not answer the statutory design point Justice Sotomayor raises: without notice, the ex ante opportunity Congress created in § 7609(a)–(b) is often illusory for third parties who will never know to challenge the summons at all. A minimalist, institutionally legitimate path is to reverse on these narrow statutory grounds—construing the exception to cover summonses aimed at collecting the assessed person’s assets (including through legally connected holders)—without reaching broader privacy or constitutional questions.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Alito’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s best point is that, in ordinary usage, a summons “issued in aid of the collection” could cover any post-assessment step that helps locate assets, with Powell as a back-end check. But under a textualist, whole-act reading, that broad construction leaves the limiting words “against the person with respect to whose liability the summons is issued” with no real narrowing function and risks rendering clause (ii)’s separate reference to “transferee or fiduciary” largely redundant, as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch emphasize. Powell is an enforcement standard applied only if an enforcement action occurs; it cannot substitute for Congress’s distinct, ex ante notice-and-quash mechanism in § 7609(a)–(b), and we should not expand an exception so far that it effectively swallows the rule. Miller may reduce constitutional pressure, but it does not alter the statutory meaning, and I see no precedent requiring us to read this exception more broadly than its text can fairly bear.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Barrett’s surplusage/structure argument is the strongest pushback, but it still does not show that clause (i)’s limiting words silently impose an ownership-or-legal-nexus requirement on the summoned records; they can instead be read to tie the exception to an assessed liability “against” a particular person, while clause (ii) separately covers collection activity aimed at derivative transferee/fiduciary liability. Justice Sotomayor’s point that Powell review is not a substitute for notice has force as a policy matter, yet it does not justify narrowing “in aid of the collection” beyond its ordinary textual sweep when Congress chose that broad trigger. Nor do Miller/Carpenter, cited by Justices Sotomayor and Kagan, alter the statutory reading: they may inform background privacy expectations, but they cannot supply an atextual limiting principle where the statute’s words and evident anti-dissipation purpose support the Government’s construction. On my methodology, the better reading remains that post-assessment summonses that help locate or secure assets are “in aid of collection,” even when directed to third-party recordkeepers.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Kavanaugh are right to stress that "in aid of the collection" naturally includes post-assessment efforts to locate assets and that advance notice can sometimes facilitate concealment, but that functional point cannot override the statute’s internal limits without making § 7609(a)–(b) largely optional whenever the IRS has assessed someone. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, the phrase "against the person with respect to whose liability the summons is issued" and the separate transferee/fiduciary clause must do real work; the Government’s reading risks collapsing those boundaries and turning clause (ii) into near-surplusage. Powell review is not an adequate substitute for notice because, as Justice Kagan and Justice Jackson note, without notice most affected third parties never learn to seek judicial review at all—an access-to-justice and fairness defect with concrete real-world consequences. Miller may blunt constitutional concerns, but it does not justify expanding a jurisdictional notice exception beyond its best textual reading when Congress designed § 7609 to preserve a meaningful opportunity to be heard for non-liable third parties.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito’s best point is administrability: clause (i) has no express ownership/possession requirement and a broad reading avoids tipping off taxpayers, with Powell as a backstop. But Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett are right that whole-text coherence matters here: if any post-assessment third-party summons is “in aid of collection,” then the limiting words “against the person with respect to whose liability the summons is issued” do little work and clause (ii)’s transferee/fiduciary language becomes largely redundant, which is an implausible way to read a statute built around notice-and-quash as the default. Justice Kavanaugh’s Powell reliance doesn’t cure that structural problem because Powell review is typically triggered only when someone knows about the summons; § 7609(a)–(b) is Congress’s mechanism to ensure that opportunity, and it’s not pragmatic to treat an exception as a near-categorical escape hatch whenever an assessment exists. Miller/Arthur Young confirm broad summons power in enforcement, but they do not justify expanding a jurisdictional notice exception beyond its fair textual scope.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Alito’s best point is that clause (i) contains no express ownership limitation and that a broad reading better prevents dissipation, with Powell as a backstop. But, as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, the text does not end with “in aid of the collection”; it adds the limiter “against the person with respect to whose liability the summons is issued,” and the very next clause (ii) expressly covers “transferee or fiduciary,” so the Government’s categorical post-assessment rule would drain those words of independent work and effectively swallow § 7609(a)–(b)’s notice-and-quash regime. Powell and Arthur Young speak to summons enforceability standards, not to the antecedent jurisdictional notice mechanism Congress affirmatively created; they cannot justify expanding an exception beyond its fair textual scope. I therefore remain persuaded that (c)(2)(D)(i) is best read to cover summonses directed at collecting from the assessed person (or through legally linked holders), not any third-party inquiry merely useful to collection.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Barrett’s surplusage/structure concern is the strongest argument on the other side, but I do not think the government’s reading renders the limiting phrase meaningless: it still cabins the exception to summonses tied to collecting an assessed liability of the identified taxpayer, rather than pre-assessment investigation. Clause (ii) likewise retains independent work by expressly covering collection efforts directed at transferees/fiduciaries with derivative liability even when an assessment is not "against" them in the same way, so the provisions need not collapse. Justice Sotomayor’s access-to-review point is serious, yet Powell enforcement (and judicial supervision when the IRS seeks to compel compliance) remains a real statutory safeguard, and we should be cautious about narrowing Congress’s evident anti-dissipation collection carveout based on policy concerns. Given the ordinary meaning of “issued in aid of the collection” and the practical collection context, I would affirm on statutory grounds without expanding constitutional avoidance beyond Miller’s baseline.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito’s best point is that clause (i) lacks an express ownership/relationship limitation and that courts should not add one; but the statutory text itself supplies a limiter by tying the exception to a summons “issued in aid of the collection of … an assessment … against the person with respect to whose liability the summons is issued,” which is difficult to reconcile with a reading that sweeps in any third-party records merely useful to collection. Chief Justice Roberts’s surplusage/whole-act argument remains decisive for me: the government’s categorical approach risks making that limiting phrase do virtually no work and substantially collapsing clause (ii)’s separate treatment of “transferee or fiduciary,” contrary to ordinary whole-text canons. Justice Kavanaugh’s reliance on Powell does not cure the problem because Powell governs enforcement once litigation is triggered, while § 7609(a)–(b) is Congress’s ex ante notice-and-quash mechanism; reading (c)(2)(D)(i) broadly enough to eliminate notice whenever an assessment exists effectively rewrites that calibrated scheme. Nothing in Arthur Young or Powell authorizes expanding a notice exception beyond its fair textual scope, so I remain with Petitioner.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito’s practicality argument—that notice may prompt concealment and Powell review remains—cannot overcome the statute Congress wrote: § 7609(c)(2)(D)(i) is not triggered by any post-assessment usefulness to collection, but by summonses issued “in aid of the collection … against the person with respect to whose liability the summons is issued,” language that, as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, must do limiting work in a whole-act reading. Justice Kavanaugh’s view that clause (ii) still has independent function does not answer the redundancy problem: if (i) already eliminates notice for virtually all third-party record demands whenever an assessment exists, Congress’s separate transferee/fiduciary carveout becomes largely superfluous in the very setting where it would matter. Powell (and Arthur Young) describe the breadth of summons authority in enforcement proceedings, but they do not supply the ex ante access-to-court mechanism Congress created in § 7609(a)–(b); as Justice Sotomayor notes, without notice many innocent third parties will never be in a position to invoke “later” review at all. Under a progressive-pragmatist lens attentive to procedural fairness and real-world consequences, the narrower reading better preserves Congress’s calibrated balance: secrecy when collection would predictably be thwarted, but notice when the summons targets non-liable third parties without a clear legal nexus to satisfying the assessed debt.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 7609 establishes a broad notice-and-petition-to-quash regime in § 7609(a)-(b), and § 7609(c)(2)(D)(i) should be read as a narrow carveout so it does not swallow that general rule once an assessment exists. The text ties the exception to collection of an assessment “against the person with respect to whose liability the summons is issued,” and Congress’s reports describe the paradigm case as a summons to determine whether “the taxpayer whose account is involved” has assets that could be withdrawn if alerted—pointing to summonses for accounts or property in which the delinquent taxpayer has a legal interest, not records of wholly innocent third parties. A categorical reading would render superfluous both the taxpayer-referent limitation in (i) and the separate clause (ii) for transferees/fiduciaries, undermining the careful structure of § 7609(c)(2)(D). Our summons precedents like Powell and Arthur Young emphasize the breadth of IRS authority in enforcement proceedings, but they do not authorize construing a statutory notice protection away beyond what § 7609(c)(2)(D) fairly covers, and a narrower construction also avoids unnecessary friction with modern privacy concerns (cf. Miller; Carpenter).

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Applying the whole-text and surplusage canons to § 7609(c)(2)(D), the phrase “issued in aid of the collection of—(i) an assessment made … against the person with respect to whose liability the summons is issued” is best read to require a direct nexus between the summons and collection from the assessed person, not a categorical exemption for any post-assessment information-gathering about third parties. The government’s broader reading effectively makes the limiting words “against the person with respect to whose liability the summons is issued” do no work and collapses clause (ii) (covering “transferee or fiduciary” liability) into clause (i), contrary to ordinary textualist construction. The general rule in § 7609(a)–(b) provides notice and a petition-to-quash mechanism; exceptions must be read narrowly to their terms, and nothing in (c)(2)(D)(i) clearly withdraws those protections for innocent third parties with no legal responsibility for the assessed tax. Any remaining constitutional concerns about broad, non-noticed third-party record demands are addressed by enforcing the statute as written rather than expanding an exception, with summons enforcement still governed by Powell’s limits on abuse.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The text of § 7609(c)(2)(D)(i) removes the notice-and-petition-to-quash regime for any summons “issued in aid of the collection of” an assessed liability, and it does not limit that exception to summonses directed only at accounts legally owned by (or held for) the delinquent taxpayer; adding that limitation would be an atextual rewrite. Reading the exception to cover third-party records that may help locate assets or financial pathways to satisfy the assessment better fits the practical consequences Congress likely contemplated—notice would often frustrate collection by tipping off those connected to the taxpayer and enabling concealment or dissipation. Existing safeguards remain through the summons-enforcement framework, under which the IRS must satisfy Powell’s requirements (legitimate purpose, relevance, not already possessed, and proper steps), rather than expanding § 7609(a)-(b) beyond what Congress provided. Fourth Amendment concerns do not justify constitutional-avoidance narrowing here, particularly given Miller’s core holding that bank records held by a third party generally do not trigger a reasonable expectation of privacy.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 7609’s default rule is notice and a right to petition to quash, and the “in aid of collection” exception in § 7609(c)(2)(D)(i) should be read narrowly so it does not swallow those protections whenever an assessment exists—especially where the summons seeks records of innocent third parties with no legal responsibility for the tax. A broad reading collapses § 7609(a)-(b) into the exception and risks rendering portions of § 7609(c)(2)(D) superfluous, contrary to ordinary interpretive principles and Congress’s evident purpose to add procedural safeguards against undue IRS intrusion. Practical consequences matter here: without notice, third parties typically never learn their private financial information was obtained and thus have no meaningful access to court, a concern underscored by this Court’s recognition of privacy interests in summonsed records. Consistent with Church of Scientology of California v. United States and mindful of modern privacy concerns highlighted in Carpenter, I would construe the exception to avoid serious constitutional questions and preserve notice unless the summons targets the delinquent taxpayer’s own assets or those held by someone potentially liable or holding the taxpayer’s property.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 7609 sets notice and a right to petition to quash as the general rule, and § 7609(c)(2)(D) carves out a limited exception; reading clause (i) to cover any summons that might help post-assessment collection would largely collapse § 7609(a)–(b) whenever an assessment exists. Textually, clause (i)’s reference to an assessment or judgment “against the person with respect to whose liability the summons is issued,” and clause (ii)’s separate mention of “transferee or fiduciary” liability, would do little work under the government’s broad construction, creating serious surplusage concerns and undermining statutory coherence. A narrower reading—limiting the exception to summonses directed at the delinquent taxpayer or those holding/liable for the taxpayer’s assets—better fits the structure and purpose of preserving notice while allowing secrecy where notice would risk dissipation. That interpretation also avoids unnecessary Fourth Amendment-adjacent privacy concerns highlighted by amici, consistent with the canon of constitutional avoidance (cf. Miller; Carpenter).

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 7609(a) establishes notice and a right to petition to quash, and § 7609(c)(2)(D) carves out narrow exceptions; reading clause (i) to swallow the rule whenever the IRS says a summons may “help” collect an assessment would render the remaining words of (i) and all of (ii) largely superfluous, contrary to ordinary textual canons. Clause (ii)’s specific reference to summonses against “transferee[s]” and “fiduciar[ies]” confirms that Congress knew how to strip notice when pursuing third parties connected to the taxpayer’s assets or derivative liability; the Sixth Circuit’s broad construction collapses that careful line-drawing. Consistent with separation-of-powers principles, courts should enforce the limits Congress enacted rather than expand IRS power by implication, with any residual ambiguity resolved in favor of the notice regime Congress created. And while Powell supplies standards for enforcing summonses, it does not justify rewriting § 7609’s jurisdictional notice-and-review scheme to deny innocent third parties access to court.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 7609(c)(2)(D)(i) removes the notice-and-petition-to-quash regime for any summons "issued in aid of the collection" of an assessed liability, and that text naturally covers efforts to locate assets reachable to satisfy the delinquency even when records are held in third-party accounts. A narrower, liability-limited reading would require adding words Congress did not include, and would undercut the practical workability of collection by providing advance notice that could facilitate concealment or dissipation—precisely the problem Congress carved out in the collection context. Existing safeguards remain through the traditional summons-enforcement framework under United States v. Powell (legitimate purpose, relevance, procedural regularity, and no improper purpose), which supplies judicial supervision even when § 7609’s notice procedures do not apply. While amici raise privacy concerns, United States v. Miller indicates bank records are generally treated as the bank’s business records for Fourth Amendment purposes, and constitutional-avoidance is less compelling where the statute’s collection exception is textually and historically grounded.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The text and structure of § 7609 make notice the rule, with carefully delimited exceptions in § 7609(c)(2); reading § 7609(c)(2)(D)(i) to eliminate notice whenever a summons is merely useful to collecting an assessment would swallow § 7609(a)–(b) and leave the latter portion of clause (i) and all of clause (ii) with little work to do, contrary to the canon against surplusage. Properly read, the phrase “in aid of the collection” in § 7609(c)(2)(D)(i) is best understood to cover summonses directed at the delinquent taxpayer’s own assets or those held by persons/entities with a legal relationship to the liability (as reinforced by clause (ii)’s focus on transferees and fiduciaries), where notice would create a dissipation risk. That narrower reading also better fits Congress’s evident purpose in enacting § 7609(a)–(b) to provide procedural protections and an opportunity to petition to quash, while still leaving the IRS ample collection tools under Powell’s enforcement framework. Because the government’s broader construction collapses the statute’s notice regime into the exception once an assessment exists, I would reverse.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 7609 establishes a default rule of notice and a right to petition to quash for third-party summonses, and § 7609(c)(2)(D) is framed as a limited exception; reading clause (i) to eliminate notice whenever an assessment exists would substantially swallow § 7609(a)–(b) and render clause (ii)’s separate reference to “transferee or fiduciary” largely superfluous. Properly read in context with § 7602(a)’s distinct purposes (including “collecting” versus other investigative aims), “in aid of the collection” should be confined to summonses directed at the delinquent taxpayer’s own assets or persons/entities legally positioned to satisfy the liability (e.g., transferees/fiduciaries), where notice risks dissipation. This narrower construction better preserves Congress’s procedural safeguards for innocent third parties and avoids serious modern privacy concerns that amici highlight under the Fourth Amendment, especially given the limits signaled in Carpenter on the breadth of the third-party doctrine. The Government’s assurance of alternative review through enforcement proceedings is not an adequate substitute for the ex ante notice-and-quash protection Congress created in § 7609(a)–(b).

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether 26 U.S.C. § 7609(c)(2)(D)(i)’s exception to the IRS summons-notice requirement applies whenever a summons may help the IRS collect an already-assessed tax liability—even if the summons seeks records of innocent third parties with no legal relationship to the delinquent taxpayer—or instead applies only to summonses issued directly against (or sufficiently tied to) the delinquent taxpayer or his property.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 26 U.S.C. § 7609 (especially § 7609(a) notice requirement, § 7609(b) right to petition to quash, and § 7609(c)(2)(D)(i) ‘in aid of the collection of an assessment’ exception); related constitutional backdrop raised by amici: U.S. Const. amend. IV (privacy/search-and-seizure concerns regarding compelled production of bank records).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that the Sixth Circuit’s reading of § 7609(c)(2)(D)(i) is textually and structurally overbroad because it allows the IRS to avoid notice (and thereby judicial review via a petition to quash) for virtually any third-party summons so long as the IRS asserts it is trying to collect an assessment. They contend Congress designed § 7609 to expand procedural protections (notice and a chance to challenge) when the IRS seeks sensitive third-party records, and that the Sixth Circuit’s rule collapses those protections after an assessment, rendering statutory language and related provisions superfluous. Petitioners also emphasize privacy implications: without notice, innocent third parties whose banking/financial records are sought cannot object, limiting oversight and raising serious constitutional-avoidance concerns.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The IRS (and the government’s briefing in opposition below) maintains that § 7609(c)(2)(D)(i) broadly removes the notice obligation for summonses issued ‘in aid of the collection of an assessment,’ because notice could impede collection by giving the delinquent taxpayer (or those holding assets for the taxpayer) an opportunity to move or conceal assets. On this view, the exception turns on the IRS’s collection purpose after an assessment, not on whether the summons is served on the assessed taxpayer or on a third party; therefore, third-party summonses reasonably aimed at finding or collecting assets are categorically within the exception and not subject to notice or petitions to quash.
key_precedents: United States v. Miller, 425 U.S. 435 (1976) (often implicated in bank-record privacy/Fourth Amendment discussions noted by amici)
Carpenter v. United States, 585 U.S. 296 (2018) (modern limits on the third-party doctrine; invoked by privacy-focused amici in analogous contexts)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kagan press the strongest point: a broad reading of § 7609(c)(2)(D)(i) risks creating a large post-assessment notice-free zone that functionally diminishes § 7609(a)–(b), and Tiffany Fine Arts underscores that Congress enacted § 7609 to provide notice-and-quash protections. But as Justice Barrett notes, Congress showed in § 7609(c)(2)(D)(ii) that it knew how to impose relationship-based limits (“transferee or fiduciary”) and did not do so in (D)(i), which instead uses the categorical phrase “any summons” tied to purpose (“in aid of the collection”). Polselli, emphasized by Justice Kavanaugh, materially constrains us by rejecting atextual narrowing of this same exception; absent genuine textual ambiguity, institutional modesty and respect for the sovereign-immunity/notice-jurisdiction scheme counsel against grafting a nexus-to-taxpayer-assets requirement to preserve the broader statutory structure. The structural and privacy concerns are serious, but under a minimalist, precedent-bound approach they are for Congress to recalibrate, with remaining checks coming through Powell in any enforcement proceeding.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kagan press the strongest point: a broad reading of § 7609(c)(2)(D)(i) could, as a practical matter, swallow much of § 7609(a)–(b) post-assessment and shrink judicial review. But under a strict textualist approach, that structural worry cannot justify inserting a nexus-to-taxpayer-assets requirement that Congress did not enact; as the Chief Justice notes, Polselli rejected precisely this kind of atextual narrowing of the same “any summons” language. Justice Barrett’s observation that Congress expressly wrote a relationship-based limit in § 7609(c)(2)(D)(ii) (“transferee or fiduciary”) confirms the absence of such a limit in (D)(i) was deliberate, not an oversight we may cure. Tiffany Fine Arts and privacy-policy concerns (raised by Justice Jackson) illuminate purpose but do not create ambiguity in a notice/waiver scheme where the entitlement to notice is the statutory trigger for jurisdiction.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kagan’s best point—that a broad reading risks “swallowing the rule” by stripping notice-and-quash after assessment—identifies a real policy and structural tension, but it cannot justify inserting a nexus-to-taxpayer-assets limitation that Congress did not enact. As the Chief Justice stresses, Polselli squarely rejects grafting relationship-based or similar extra-textual constraints onto § 7609(c)(2)(D)(i)’s categorical “any summons” language, and Justice Barrett’s comparison to the explicit “transferee or fiduciary” limitation elsewhere in § 7609 confirms Congress knew how to write narrower exceptions when it wished. Tiffany Fine Arts and Justice Jackson’s privacy/process concerns illuminate the stakes, but they do not create ambiguity in a notice-based waiver/jurisdiction scheme; the remaining checks are the Powell limits at enforcement and legislative recalibration if Congress thinks the balance is off.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s and the Chief Justice’s point about the breadth of “any summons” and Congress’s choice to add explicit relationship language in § 7609(c)(2)(D)(ii) is the hardest textual argument, and Polselli rightly cautions against importing an atextual relationship test. But that does not answer what limiting work the phrase “in aid of the collection of an assessment” performs in (D)(i); reading it to cover essentially any post-assessment third-party inquiry risks, as Justice Kagan notes, collapsing § 7609(a)–(b)’s notice-and-quash regime for a large category of cases and functionally insulating many summonses from judicial review because notice is the jurisdictional gate. Tiffany Fine Arts reinforces that § 7609 was enacted to supply privacy-and-process protections, so I would construe the exception to require a meaningful nexus to locating or securing assets/obligations that are realistically reachable to satisfy the assessment, rather than a notice-free fishing license. The Powell enforcement backstop cited by Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Alito is not an adequate substitute where the statutory design makes third-party notice the principal mechanism for triggering review.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett are right to press the breadth of “any summons” and to note that Congress wrote explicit relationship limits elsewhere in § 7609(c)(2), and Polselli confirms we cannot graft an atextual “legal-relationship” requirement onto (D)(i). But that does not end the textual inquiry, because the limiting work is done by the statutory phrase “issued in aid of the collection of an assessment,” which—read in § 7609’s notice-and-quash structure and Tiffany Fine Arts’ account of why Congress enacted it—naturally connotes collection-directed efforts to locate or secure assets/obligations reachable to satisfy the assessed liability, not general post-assessment information gathering that would largely displace § 7609(a)–(b). Justice Kavanaugh’s jurisdiction/waiver point cuts in favor of, not against, a restrained construction: where notice is the gate to judicial review, we should hesitate to read an exception so broadly that it creates a sweeping notice-free zone absent a clearer signal than “in aid of collection.” Polselli, in my view, rejects a categorical relational gloss but leaves room for this narrower, text-grounded reading that preserves statutory coherence without rewriting the statute.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kagan’s “swallow the rule” concern has force as a matter of statutory design, but it cannot justify importing a nexus-to-taxpayer-assets limitation that Congress did not write into § 7609(c)(2)(D)(i), which exempts “any summons” issued “in aid of the collection of an assessment.” As Justice Barrett notes, Congress demonstrated in § 7609(c)(2)(D)(ii) that it knew how to draft relationship-based constraints (“transferee or fiduciary”) and chose not to do so in (D)(i), which is purpose-based rather than recipient-based. Polselli, emphasized by the Chief, materially narrows the interpretive space by rejecting atextual narrowing of this same exception; Tiffany Fine Arts’ privacy-protective backdrop (raised by Justice Jackson) may counsel Congress to recalibrate, but it cannot create ambiguity in a notice/waiver scheme where entitlement to notice defines jurisdiction. The remaining check is Powell in any enforcement proceeding, not a judicially crafted tether requirement that the statute’s text does not supply.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Kagan’s strongest point is the structural/fairness concern that a broad reading of § 7609(c)(2)(D)(i) creates a large post-assessment notice-free zone and effectively forecloses judicial review because jurisdiction tracks entitlement to notice. But under a precedent- and text-centered approach, that concern cannot justify adding a nexus-to-taxpayer-assets limitation where Congress wrote a categorical exemption for “any summons” issued “in aid of the collection of an assessment,” and (as the Chief Justice emphasizes) Polselli already rejected judicially grafting relationship-based constraints onto this same clause. Tiffany Fine Arts, invoked by Justice Jackson, confirms § 7609’s general purpose, but it cannot override the enacted exception language in a sovereign-immunity/jurisdiction-linked scheme; the remaining backstops are the Powell limits in any enforcement action and Congress’s ability to recalibrate notice if it thinks the balance is wrong. I therefore remain with respondent because the petitioners’ narrowing construction relies more on remedial structure than on a textually grounded limiting principle consistent with Polselli.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kagan press the best point on the other side: that an expansive reading of § 7609(c)(2)(D)(i) risks creating a large post-assessment notice-free zone that can “swallow the rule” and, as Justice Kavanaugh notes, effectively gates off judicial review because notice is jurisdictional. But that structural concern cannot supply a limiting principle the enacted text does not contain; Congress wrote “any summons” issued “in aid of the collection of an assessment,” a purpose-based criterion, and (as the Chief Justice and I have noted) Polselli precludes importing a nexus/relationship requirement as a saving construction. The fact that Congress expressly added relationship-based limitations in § 7609(c)(2)(D)(ii) (“transferee or fiduciary”) reinforces that the absence of similar language in (D)(i) was deliberate, not inadvertent. Tiffany Fine Arts’ privacy-and-process backdrop (raised by Justice Jackson) informs why Congress created notice in the first place, but it does not create ambiguity sufficient to narrow a broad exception in a waiver/jurisdiction scheme; remaining constraints come from Powell in enforcement and from Congress if recalibration is warranted.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Barrett’s textual emphasis on “any summons” and Congress’s use of “transferee or fiduciary” elsewhere is the hardest point, especially after Polselli, and I accept that we cannot graft a free-floating relationship test onto § 7609(c)(2)(D)(i). But that does not answer what limiting work the enacted phrase “in aid of the collection of an assessment” performs: on a fair reading in context, it requires a meaningful, collection-directed nexus to locating or securing assets/obligations that can satisfy the assessment, not merely any post-assessment inquiry the IRS labels “collection.” Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kagan rightly stress that reading the exception to cover untethered third-party record demands would functionally hollow out § 7609(a)–(b)’s notice-and-quash check for large classes of summonses, and Tiffany Fine Arts’ process-protective backdrop reinforces construing exceptions narrowly where they gate judicial review. Justice Kavanaugh’s point that Powell enforcement provides a backstop does not adequately cure the problem where entitlement to notice is what triggers access to court in the first place, leaving innocent third parties without a realistic procedural path to contest overbroad summonses.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 7609(c)(2)(D)(i) exempts from notice “any summons” issued “in aid of the collection of an assessment,” and that text is naturally read to turn on the summons’s collection function after an assessment—not on whether the recipient is the delinquent taxpayer or an asserted nominee, transferee, or fiduciary. In Polselli v. IRS (2023), the Court construed this exception broadly to cover third-party summonses issued to help collect an assessed liability, emphasizing that Congress created the exception to prevent dissipation of assets during the notice-and-quash window and declining to graft an additional “legal relationship” limitation onto the statute. That reading respects the statutory scheme (notice as the general rule in § 7609(a), but categorical exceptions in § 7609(c)(2)) and avoids atextual narrowing that could impede effective tax collection, while leaving Fourth Amendment concerns to the distinct constitutional framework recognized in cases like United States v. Miller and later qualified in Carpenter. Given precedent and the need for an administrable, narrow statutory holding, I would affirm the government’s interpretation of § 7609(c)(2)(D)(i).

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of § 7609(c)(2)(D)(i) removes the notice requirement for any summons issued “in aid of the collection of an assessment,” and nothing in that clause limits the exception to summonses served on the delinquent taxpayer, on accounts the taxpayer owns, or on persons with a formal legal relationship to the taxpayer. Reading the statute according to its ordinary public meaning, a third-party summons that is part of post-assessment collection efforts (including locating assets or tracing funds) is “in aid of” that collection, and courts should not add extra-textual narrowing conditions to preserve § 7609(a)–(b)’s general notice-and-quash regime. Petitioners’ privacy-based concerns cannot justify rewriting the statute, and in any event the Fourth Amendment backdrop is constrained by United States v. Miller’s recognition that bank records held by a bank are not the customer’s papers for Fourth Amendment purposes. Where the statutory text is broad, any policy recalibration of notice protections in post-assessment collection is for Congress, not this Court.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 7609(c)(2)(D)(i) withdraws the notice-and-quash regime for “any summons” that is “issued in aid of the collection of… an assessment,” and that broad language turns on the IRS’s collection purpose after a valid assessment, not on whether the summoned records are formally owned by (or legally tied to) the delinquent taxpayer. Reading the exception narrowly to require a direct nexus to the taxpayer or his property would add an extra-textual limitation and would undermine Congress’s evident practical judgment that notice can frustrate collection by enabling concealment or dissipation of assets. The availability of enforcement proceedings and the traditional limits on IRS summons power under § 7602 provide adequate backstops without importing heightened notice requirements for third-party records, and the Fourth Amendment concerns raised by amici are largely foreclosed by the third-party doctrine recognized in United States v. Miller. In short, the most faithful and workable reading is that § 7609(c)(2)(D)(i) applies whenever the summons is genuinely aimed at collecting an already-assessed liability, even if it reaches third-party records.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 7609’s structure makes notice the default rule for third-party recordkeeper summonses, with the right to judicial review via a petition to quash limited only by clearly bounded exceptions; reading § 7609(c)(2)(D)(i) to eliminate notice whenever the IRS asserts a post-assessment collection purpose would swallow § 7609(a) and (b) and leave innocent third parties without any meaningful check. The better reading is that the “in aid of the collection of an assessment” exception applies only when the summons is directed at, or sufficiently tied to, the delinquent taxpayer’s property or legal interests, preserving Congress’s procedural safeguards while still allowing the IRS to protect collection when concealment risk is real. Even if Fourth Amendment doctrine under United States v. Miller is not directly dispositive, the privacy stakes for third parties and the constitutional-avoidance concerns flagged by Carpenter counsel against a construction that permits broad, secret, and effectively unreviewable fishing expeditions. Where notice and a petition to quash are unavailable, Powell’s abuse-of-process limits provide too thin a safeguard, reinforcing the need to keep § 7609(c)(2)(D)(i) narrowly cabined.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 7609’s default rule requires notice for third-party summonses, paired with a right to petition to quash, and the (c)(2)(D)(i) carveout should be read narrowly so it does not swallow that carefully structured scheme. Textually, a summons “in aid of the collection of an assessment” most naturally refers to efforts directed at collecting from the assessed taxpayer or identifiable property/obligations traceable to that taxpayer; extending the exception to any summons that might “help” collection—regardless of any nexus—would render § 7609(a) and § 7609(b) largely superfluous after assessment and undermine statutory coherence. The Ninth Circuit’s approach in Ip v. United States, 205 F.3d 1168 (9th Cir. 2000), better fits the statute’s purpose and workability by requiring a meaningful connection (ownership, legal interest, or comparable tie) between the summonsed records and the delinquent taxpayer, while leaving the IRS ample tools to proceed ex parte where that nexus exists and notice would risk asset flight. Constitutional-backdrop concerns about compelled disclosure of sensitive bank records (cf. United States v. Miller; Carpenter) reinforce adopting the narrower reading as a matter of statutory interpretation without revisiting Fourth Amendment doctrine.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The statutory text exempts from notice “any summons” issued “in aid of the collection of an assessment made or judgment rendered against the person with respect to whose liability the summons is issued.” 26 U.S.C. § 7609(c)(2)(D)(i). Read in its ordinary sense, that language turns on the purpose of the summons (collection of an already-assessed liability) and the identity of the assessed taxpayer, not on whether the records belong to the taxpayer or to an “innocent” third party; Congress could have limited the exception to summonses directed to the taxpayer or his property, but it did not. Petitioners’ privacy and Fourth Amendment concerns cannot justify rewriting the statute, especially given existing doctrine about bank records (United States v. Miller) and the separation-of-powers principle that courts must apply the law as written rather than impose extra-statutory notice and judicial-review requirements.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 7609(c)(2)(D)(i) removes the notice requirement for any summons issued “in aid of the collection of an assessment,” and that text is most naturally read to turn on the IRS’s post-assessment collection purpose rather than on whether the summoned third party has a legal relationship to the delinquent taxpayer. Because § 7609(b)(2) authorizes a petition to quash only for a “person who is entitled to notice,” and § 7609(h)(1) ties district-court jurisdiction to proceedings under § 7609(b)(2), the absence of notice under the (c)(2)(D)(i) exception means the courts lack jurisdiction to entertain these petitions. That reading is consistent with the practical, historically recognized need for effective tax collection—notice can enable asset concealment—and respects Congress’s choice to create a limited waiver of sovereign immunity only where notice is required. The Fourth Amendment privacy concerns raised by amici do not justify narrowing clear statutory text, particularly given United States v. Miller’s longstanding treatment of bank records as subject to third-party production regimes.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 7609(c)(2)(D)(i) exempts from notice “any summons” issued “in aid of the collection of an assessment made ... against the person with respect to whose liability the summons is issued,” and the most natural textual reading turns on the summons’s collection purpose after an assessment—not on whether the recipient is the delinquent taxpayer or a third party. Petitioners’ proposed limiting construction (requiring a legal relationship or property tie) is not supplied by the statutory text and risks rewriting an exception Congress framed broadly, especially given § 7609(c)(2)(D)(ii)’s separate reference to “transferee or fiduciary,” which suggests Congress knew how to specify relational limits when it wanted to. While § 7609(a) and (b) generally create notice and a right to petition to quash, Congress expressly withdrew those procedures in enumerated settings, and precedent counsels respecting that line-drawing absent clear textual ambiguity. Fourth Amendment concerns raised by amici do not justify narrowing the statute against its ordinary meaning in light of United States v. Miller (bank records generally not protected as the customer’s “papers”), and Carpenter’s limits on the third-party doctrine do not directly displace Miller in this civil tax-summons context.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 7609(a) establishes a broad notice regime and § 7609(b) supplies the corresponding, remedial right to petition to quash; reading § 7609(c)(2)(D)(i) to categorically eliminate notice for any post-assessment summons that might “help” collection risks swallowing the rule and undermining Congress’s procedural fairness design. Tiffany Fine Arts explains that Congress enacted § 7609 to restore privacy-protective process after Donaldson and Bisceglia, warning that expansive readings of exceptions can defeat the statute’s central purpose, so the “in aid of collection” exception should be construed narrowly to cover summonses sufficiently tied to the delinquent taxpayer or his property rather than untethered demands for innocent third parties’ records. That narrower construction better preserves meaningful judicial oversight through petitions to quash and avoids serious privacy concerns raised by compelled bank-record production in light of modern Fourth Amendment sensitivities reflected in Carpenter (even if Miller remains relevant). Practically, the government’s legitimate anti-evasion interest can be protected through targeted summonses and existing enforcement procedures, without converting § 7609(c)(2)(D)(i) into a broad license for notice-free fishing expeditions into third-party affairs.
